title: What is known about 1RB---_1RC0LE_1RD1RF_1LB0LB_0RD0LD_0RC0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB---_1RC0LE_1RD1RF_1LB0LB_0RD0LD_0RC0RA.
intro: This six-state, two-symbol Turing machine was one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project; an outside Rocq proof has since shown that it halts when started on a blank tape. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Decided by an outside Rocq proof: it halts. Busycoq pull request 81 (Alex Havrilla of DeepMind, 2026-11-17) proves this in Rocq, and we compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch: it uses only the 25 PrimInt63 / Uint63 axioms of Coq's primitive 63-bit integers (Print Assumptions), and its transition table is this machine. By their count it halts after about 1098,832 steps. It is their proof, on busycoq's definitions of a machine and of halting, and busycoq's maintainer merged it into the BB6 branch (commit 9c078ca) on 26 November 2026. Everything else on this page is what this repository found on its own, which by itself leaves the question open.

What this repository found on its own. Before the proof, simulation showed the machine moving material, one word every two visits, from one long run of a periodic word into another; each phase leaves a marker behind, and the runs it leaves have lengths in ratios close to 3/2. The proof explains this: those runs are the entries of a stack that each pass of the head halves and sums (see the explainer).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (A1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 73,042 cells have been visited and 40,382 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.444). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: Transfer phases
claims.text: At the left-end visits in state D the first run loses one period-6 word and the second gains one period-9 word per round (750 per 1,500 rounds from 5.5·10<sup>8</sup> to 8.0·10<sup>8</sup> steps); the frozen runs to the right have lengths 133, 88, 58, 38, 15.

claims.title: Transfer phases
claims.text: At the left-end visits in state D the first run loses one period-6 word and the second gains one period-9 word every two visits (750 per 1,500 visits from 5.5·10<sup>8</sup> to 8.0·10<sup>8</sup> steps); the frozen runs to the right have lengths 133, 88, 58, 38, 15.

claims.title: Transfer phases
claims.text: At the left-end visits in state D the first run loses one period-6 word and the second gains one period-9 word every two visits (750 per 1,500 visits from 5.5·10<sup>8</sup> to 8.0·10<sup>8</sup> steps); the frozen runs to the right have lengths 133, 88, 58, 38, 15.

claims.title: No halt in the first 5.77×10<sup>10</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: Observed, not proved: the accelerated simulator rsim.py ran 5.77×1010 steps from blank tape without reaching a halting transition. Its tape, state and head position were equal to those of a plain C simulator at 6 checkpoints, the last at 1.00×1010 steps. Of these steps, the part after the last checkpoint rests on the simulator alone, including 9 trip-level jumps: a jump applies many identical round trips at once after seeing the same tape shape recur with constant count changes, which is validated against direct simulation but not proved.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape? (this repository’s own ledger)
claims.text: Not decided by the results on this page alone. It is decided outside: busycoq pull request 81 proves that it halts (see the verdict).

explainer.lede: It halts, after about 1098,832 steps. Right of the head’s home the tape is a stack of long runs of the word 100001000, separated by short markers. Each pass of the head puts a new run at the front about one and a half times longer than the old front run, and halves the runs it crosses; after 192,575 passes a marker that means “stop” reaches the front and the machine halts.

facts.text: between consecutive frozen runs, found here by simulation; the proof shows why: each pass halves a run and adds the half to the next one.
No halt in the C simulator; 73,042 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
No halt in the accelerated simulator (observed, not proved; checked against direct simulation up to 1.00×10<sup>10</sup> steps).

sections.heading: A stack of counters that halve and add
html: The proof is busycoq pull request 81 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind. We compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1; besides Coq’s own rules it uses only the standard axioms of Coq’s built-in 63-bit integers, which it needs to do arithmetic on very large numbers quickly.

The shape of the tape. Write R9 for the nine-cell word 100001000 and R9n for it written n times. At the moments the proof watches, the machine is in state C, eleven 1s lie to its left, and to its right come 00000 and then a list of runs R9n1 d1 R9n2 d2 …, where each d is one of seven short marker words (from 3 to 13 cells long). The proof calls this list a stack of pairs (n, d). Three markers, P1 to P3, let the head pass; four, W1 to W4, act as walls that turn it back.

One macro step. From this position the head makes many trips back and forth. It works through the stack from the front, turning R9 words into shorter words on its left, until it meets the first wall marker. Then it comes back, and every run it passed is replaced by half of itself, the remainder (odd or even) choosing the marker that follows it; the halves are added up into one new run at the front. In the simplest case, a stack that starts with n words and a wall W1, with n even, becomes one that starts with n + n/2 + 3 words, then n/2 words, and the run behind loses one word. So the front run grows by a factor of about 3/2 per step, and the runs left behind keep ratios close to 3/2: the 908, 302, 200, 133 and 88 that this repository found by simulation are such entries.

How it stops. The wall W2 makes a W3 when the head comes back, and W3 makes a W4. When the first wall the head meets is W4 and the run behind it has at least two words, the machine is 31 steps from reading a 1 in state A, which has no transition, so it halts. Starting from a blank tape, 11,243 steps and four macro steps reach the stack (154, W1), (30, P3), (10, W2), (5, P2), (3, P2), (2, W1); after 192,575 macro steps from there the W4 case comes up. By then the counts are about 164,000 bits long, and the raw machine has run about 1098,832 steps.

What is proved and what is computed. The rules for sweeping across any number of R6 or R9 words, and the three kinds of bounce that make up a macro step, are proved for every length by induction. A theorem then says that a short program on the stack (stackStep) does exactly what the machine does, so one run of the program stands for one macro step of the machine. Another says that entries deep in the stack, which a step does not reach, can be dropped without changing the outcome. The computer checks the rest with Coq’s vm_compute: the first 11,243 steps, a few dozen fixed short pieces of tape, and the 192,575 program steps on big numbers, done in 3,008 blocks of 64 steps that keep the first 24 stack entries.

sections.heading: Moving material between runs
html: The tape is made of long runs of a few periodic words, mostly 100010000 (9 cells) and 000100 or 000001 (6 cells), separated by short markers. Every second time the head, in state D, comes back to the left end, one more word has moved from the first run to the next one: the first run shrinks by one word of 6 cells and the second grows by one word of 9 cells. When the first run is empty a new phase begins with other words.

Each phase leaves a marker and a run behind it. The runs further right are frozen; their lengths, 133, 88, 58, 38 and 15 for one kind of word, shrink by factors close to 3/2. This repository saw that pattern before the proof and guessed a Collatz-like map behind it; the proof above gives the exact rule, a stack whose entries are halved and added.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.444). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 73,042 cells (46,778 left of the start, 32 right), with a density of 1s of 0.553.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the stack described in the proof section.

summary: Phases of transfer between long runs of period-6 and period-9 words; the frozen runs it leaves behind shrink by ratios close to 3/2, the mark of a Collatz-like map (not extracted). Decided outside: busycoq PR 81 (merged 26 Nov 2026) proves in Rocq that it halts (compiled here).
